title: Forgets to eat
hook: Confucius describes himself as someone so eager to learn he forgets his food (Analects 7.18)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Qing, the woodworker who fasted until reward and praise fell away. Your line was forget the prize. Today, another kind of forgetting, from another Chinese teacher.

Somebody asks your friend what you're really like, and your friend says nothing. Just stands there. Later, you hear about it. That's the scene in the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. A nobleman, the Duke of She, asks one of Confucius's students, Zilu, what kind of man his teacher is. Zilu doesn't answer. When Confucius finds out, he doesn't scold. He tells Zilu what he could have said, and the portrait he offers of himself isn't of a sage or a statesman. Today's word is the student who stayed silent: Zilu.
screen: `WHAT'S HE REALLY LIKE?` → `ZILU SAYS NOTHING.` → `A MAN WHO FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: First, the description, in paraphrase. Why didn't you tell him, Confucius says, that I'm simply a man who, in his eagerness, forgets his food; who, in the joy of it, forgets his worries; and who doesn't notice old age coming on? Three forgettings: food, sorrow, age. Second, what's being chased. The line itself just says eagerness, but Legge and the commentators read it as eagerness to learn. Not power, not money: the steady work of study and practice that runs through the Analects. For Confucius, that work wasn't a chore to get through. In this passage, it's what he loses himself in. Third, notice the joy. He doesn't forget food because he's grimly disciplined. The joy of it makes him forget his troubles. The eagerness comes first, and the forgetting follows. Nobody has to hide his tools or take away his plate. The hours just go. Fourth, how this sits next to yesterday. Qing the woodworker had to fast for days to forget reward and praise. Confucius describes something that arrives on its own when the work itself is loved. Two roads to the same quiet place, where the clock and the stomach go silent for a while. And the honest part: the Analects doesn't recommend skipping meals. Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food. This is a portrait of absorption, not a rule about lunch. It can turn up anywhere: a puzzle, a garden, a song, and suddenly the window has gone dark.
screen: `FOOD, SORROW, AGE: FORGOTTEN.` · `WHAT HE CHASES IS LEARNING.` · `JOY COMES FIRST.` · `ABSORPTION, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Think back to a time you lost track of the hours doing something, recently or long ago, and let the memory fill in: what you were doing, where you sat, what your hands did. Then ask whether something like it is within reach today, even for twenty minutes. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own tradition's words.
Zilu. The student who didn't answer when asked what kind of man Confucius was, and what Confucius told him he could have said. Today's word.
Your line: forget the hours. Joy first, and the forgetting follows. Day nine hundred two, done.

screen: `DAY 902 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IT COSTS IN LIFE.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Analects, in Confucian schools and families and in classrooms, turn to this passage as Confucius's own picture of a life given to learning.

chat.says: If not a sage, what did Confucius say he was really like?
options: A man so eager he forgets to eat, forgets his worries in the joy, and doesn't notice age.
A strict man who skipped meals on purpose to train himself to need very little.
A statesman who worked so hard for the ruler that he had no time left for joy.
chat.meaning: In this passage Confucius pictures himself forgetting food, worries and age out of eager joy: absorption, not a rule about skipping meals.

Zilu.meaning: a student of Confucius who stayed silent

Duke of She.meaning: a nobleman who asked Zilu about Confucius

Legge.meaning: a translator of the Analects into English

notes: Analects 7.18 paraphrased rather than quoting Legge, to avoid misquoting. Numbering differs between editions (7.18 Legge / 7.19 others).
'Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food' refers to Analects book 10 (e.g. 10.8); confirm reference.
Trapdoor calls it 'a passage where Confucius describes himself': softened from 'a rare passage'.
Teach ends on absorption examples rather than any claim about how many people experience it.
Editor: cut the uncited claim that the Analects was gathered by his followers.

Audit: 7.18 does not name the object of Confucius's eagerness (fa fen); Legge supplies '(of knowledge)' in brackets. The teach now says the line says eagerness and that Legge and commentators read it as learning, instead of presenting 'learning' as the text's own word. Keeper: confirm 'the commentators' phrasing.
